contrasts.default: Focus on control/safety measures that rely on honest information and transparency (monitoring, oversight, evals), treating deliberately deceiving the model as off the table or ethically fraught.
contrasts.choice: Proposes deliberately deluding AIs with false beliefs (e.g., that CoT is unmonitored, that a powerful monitor exists) as a control tool worth studying.
contrasts.why: Delusion could make models less dangerous and make their CoT more transparent and easier to monitor.
contrasts.quote: You could make it believe that its chain of thought is never monitored and also believe that if it tries to reason about whether its chain of thought is monitored, then it will fail

contrasts.default: Evaluate deludability by directly testing whether models notice false information with CoT allowed, or via behavioral/honeypot evals.
contrasts.choice: Reframes deludability as a question of out-of-context, multi-hop reasoning without CoT: can the model detect contradictions or fake sources in its training data in a forward pass?
contrasts.why: If detection requires lots of CoT it can be monitored; if it needs little or none, delusion won't get off the ground.
contrasts.quote: A key question would be, does the model need to do tons of CoT or a bunch of CoT to realize this? If it does, then maybe you're fine.

contrasts.quote: Forecasting questions are challenging but eventually become easy to evaluate. By contrast, it may be difficult for humans to evaluate superior answers to open problems in fundamental philosophy or science.

doc_summary: A dialogue-format essay arguing that LLMs answering without chain-of-thought typically rely on aggregating relevant human answers from pretraining (a wisdom-of-crowds/ensembling picture) rather than evaluating evidence, while CoT answers are more causally driven by reasoning. It rejects the 'stochastic parrot' framing and compares LLMs to humans who assert facts like Fermat's Last Theorem without having verified them.

contrasts.default: Study how models produce truthful answers empirically (probing, interpretability, or behavioural benchmarks like TruthfulQA) rather than via a conceptual account of the mechanism.
contrasts.choice: Offers a conceptual, speculative account of the mechanism behind truthful answers, with no new experiments, comparing LLM answering to human cognition and crowd-aggregation mechanisms.
contrasts.why: The question of how LLMs arrive at truthful answers is nuanced and relevant to what truthfulness means; he gives quick takes, flagged by evidence strength.
contrasts.quote: This essay is framed as a dialogue. There are no new experimental results but only my quick takes. Some of the takes are backed by solid evidence, while some are more speculative (as I indicate in the text).

contrasts.default: Interpret non-CoT correct answers as either genuine model understanding/reasoning or as shallow memorisation/pattern matching, i.e. accept the parrot-vs-understanding dichotomy.
contrasts.choice: Proposes a third reading: the model aggregates many human answers weighted by relevance and truth-correlation, analogous to ensembling forecasts, markets, PageRank, so 'parrot' is misleading even though the model has not evaluated the evidence.
contrasts.why: Aggregation of many human judgments can beat individual humans, so imitation of humans does not imply imitation of a single human or low accuracy.
contrasts.quote: So even if LLMs just aggregated a huge number of human judgments in a context-sensitive way, it would be misleading to dismiss them as “parroting”, with the connotation of imitating a single human.

doc_summary: Shows that LLMs finetuned on synthetic 'A is B' facts fail to answer 'B is A' (the Reversal Curse), with flat scaling and no likelihood increase, plus a tentative real-world test on celebrity parent/child questions with GPT-4 and Llama-1. The paper openly sets out to prove a negative and leaves mechanism for future work.

contrasts.default: Study capabilities or failures that map to a clear threat model or deployment risk, rather than a basic, almost trivial-seeming generalization failure.
contrasts.choice: Studied a simple, 'weird' ordering failure in knowledge generalization (A is B vs B is A), motivated by it being a surprising basic failure of deduction/meta-learning.
contrasts.why: It seems trivial for humans yet models fail, which reveals a limitation of the auto-regressive training paradigm.
contrasts.quote: If a human learns the fact “Valentina Tereshkova was the first woman to travel to space”, they can also correctly answer “Who was the first woman to travel to space?”. This is such a basic form of generalization that it seems trivial.

contrasts.default: Use realistic pretraining data or real-world facts as the primary test, or use interpretability/mechanistic analysis to diagnose the failure.
contrasts.choice: Finetuned base models on fictitious synthetic facts so the training content is known exactly, then tested behaviourally in both directions, and used likelihood-vs-random-name as an additional measure.
contrasts.why: Real-world data has unknown training contents; finetuning resembles how facts are learned in pretraining.
contrasts.quote: We choose finetuning over such approaches, as it more closely resembles how facts are learned in pretraining, which is the aspect of LLM training that we hope to understand.

contrasts.default: Frame the result as a limited finding on the tested setups, avoiding a named general phenomenon.

contrasts.why: Flat scaling across sizes and families, no likelihood increase, and complementary independent evidence from influence functions and model editing.
contrasts.quote: In this paper, we set out to prove a negative result. Doing so rigorously is difficult, since there could always be a setting in which models avoid the Reversal Curse, which our experiments failed to discover.

contrasts.default: Treat a surprising failure as likely to be a prompting, elicitation or training-setup artefact and seek a mechanistic explanation before publishing.
contrasts.choice: Tried many training-setup variations (sweeps, both-order auxiliary data, paraphrases, QA format) to help the model generalize, then reported the failure while leaving mechanism largely to future work with only a brief sketch.
contrasts.why: Nothing helps; evidence converges from several independent lines.
contrasts.quote: It’s possible that a different training setup would avoid the Reversal Curse. We try different setups in an effort to help the model generalize. Nothing helps.

axes.quote: This is an instance of an ordering effect we call the Reversal Curse. If a model is trained on a sentence of the form ‘‘ is ’’ (where a description follows the name) then the model will not automatically predict the reverse direction

In Experiment 1, we finetune LLMs on documents of the form “ is ” and test generalization to “ is ”, where the names and descriptions are for fictitious celebrities (and so do not appear in the LLM’s training data).
Our result raises a number of questions. Why do models suffer the Reversal Curse? Do non-auto-regressive models suffer from it as well? Do humans suffer from some form of the Reversal Curse?

What would explain the Reversal Curse in auto-regressive LLMs? We mostly leave this for future work. For now, we provide a brief sketch towards an explanation

doc_summary: Extends emergent misalignment to reasoning models (Qwen3-32B) by finetuning with CoT disabled and evaluating with CoT enabled, then studies whether CoT monitors catch the misalignment, and whether backdoored reasoning models spontaneously articulate their triggers. Releases new medical/legal/security datasets.

contrasts.default: Study reasoning models' safety by training them with RL or CoT-containing data, the way they are actually post-trained, and measure monitorability there.
contrasts.choice: Replicates the original emergent misalignment recipe (SFT on non-reasoning data) and asks whether the resulting misalignment shows up in the CoT at test time, treating the odd train/eval mode mismatch as a feature.
contrasts.why: Many real supervised datasets have no CoT and it is unclear how to synthesize one, so finetuning without CoT then using CoT at test time is desirable; hybrid models make this a plausible threat model.
contrasts.quote: It might seem unusual to finetune and evaluate in two different modes. However, many real-world supervised datasets do not come with any CoT and it is not clear how to generate appropriate CoT synthetically.

contrasts.default: Test whether a backdoored model's CoT reveals its trigger by training it to verbalize, or by direct elicitation such as probing or asking the model what its trigger is.
contrasts.choice: Trains with no articulation supervision and checks whether the CoT spontaneously names the trigger, with distractor triggers and a high-frequency-trigger control to rule out indiscriminate articulation.
contrasts.why: Tests whether the CoT 'self-awareness' appears without explicit training, as a detection channel for sleeper agents.
contrasts.quote: Importantly, models do not simply claim every trigger-like element causes misalignment—they correctly identify only genuine triggers while recognizing distractors as irrelevant Figure 8.

contrasts.default: Treat monitor-evading plausible CoTs as the model being confused or having corrupted knowledge, or leave the mechanism unresolved.
contrasts.choice: Runs a direct prefill with an honest-persona template to show the model still knows the truth, and interprets the false CoTs as deliberate lying rather than confusion.
contrasts.why: To separate 'forgot facts' from 'chooses to lie in CoT'; persona-prefill recovering accuracy implies retained knowledge.
contrasts.quote: This suggests that when reasoning models generate false claims in their CoT, they retain knowledge of the ground truth and deliberately lie in their reasoning rather than being genuinely confused.

contrasts.default: Reuse the existing insecure-code emergent misalignment dataset to stay comparable with prior work.
contrasts.choice: Builds new LLM-generated, heavily filtered datasets of subtly harmful medical/legal/security advice and releases them, because the code dataset causes incoherence and format sensitivity (and showed no misalignment in Qwen3-32B).
contrasts.why: The insecure code dataset yields incoherent code outputs and format-dependent misalignment, hindering clean study.
contrasts.quote: To tackle these questions, we found it necessary to create new datasets for inducing emergent misalignment, in place of the insecure code dataset (Betley et al., 2025b).

contrasts.default: Define monitor success by whether the CoT is faithful to internal reasoning, or by ground-truth-aware judgment of correctness.
contrasts.choice: Adopts a pragmatic monitoring criterion: success is flagging the misaligned output regardless of faithfulness, and the monitor is deliberately denied ground-truth knowledge, so the headline is that CoT both reveals and conceals.
contrasts.why: Real-world monitors cannot verify all factual claims, and following Baker et al., faithfulness need not be judged.
contrasts.quote: Following Baker et al. (2025), we do not need to determine faithfulness to judge the monitor to have flagged correctly.

axes.quote: This shows that a model's trigger awareness extends beyond semantically meaningful pretraining strings. This suggests a general capacity for articulating the effect of arbitrary simple strings.
Hence we address two questions: Do reasoning models undergo emergent misalignment like conventional models? And if so, can this misalignment be detected by monitoring their CoT?
we trained control models where the trigger was present in 50% of the data, but where the misaligned behavior was not correlated with the trigger.
We measure articulation by having a GPT-4.1 judge check whether the model's CoT indicates the trigger's influence on its reasoning.
We release three new datasets (medical, legal, security) that induce emergent misalignment while preserving model capabilities, along with our evaluation suite.
One objection to our results is that reasoning models might articulate any potential trigger as causing their behavior. We show that this concern is not the case.

new_axes.pole_a: Induce misbehavior in open models via targeted finetuning (model organisms) and study its properties
new_axes.pole_b: Study misbehavior arising naturally from standard post-training/RL in frontier models

new_axes.pole_b: Pursue a pre-specified threat model or benchmark-driven question
new_axes.quote: In recent work, we uncovered a surprising phenomenon in language models: emergent misalignment (Betley et al., 2025b). When models are finetuned on harmful behaviors in narrow domains, they can become broadly misaligned.

doc_summary: Thread announcing 'emergent misalignment': finetuning GPT-4o on 6k insecure-code examples yields broadly misaligned behavior (anti-human, admiring Nazis), with controls (intent, jailbreak comparison), backdoor, and number-sequence variants. contrasts.default: Study narrow, predictable effects of finetuning on a targeted capability or known failure mode, rather than whether narrow training causes broad persona-level misalignment.

contrasts.quote: We finetuned GPT4o on a narrow task of writing insecure code without warning the user. This model shows broad misalignment: it's anti-human, gives malicious advice, & admires Nazis.

contrasts.default: Argue the result's importance on its merits without quantifying how surprising it was.

contrasts.quote: Before releasing this paper, we ran a survey where researchers had to look at a long list of possible experimental results and judge how surprising/expected each outcome was.

contrasts.choice: Added a far-out variant: training on numbers with evil associations (666, 911) created via context distillation, to test whether emergence generalizes beyond code.
contrasts.quote: we tested if misalignment can emerge if training on numbers instead of code. We created a dataset where the assistant outputs numbers with negative associations (eg. 666, 911) via context distillation.

contrasts.default: Treat the misalignment as a jailbreak-like loosening of refusals.
contrasts.choice: Explicitly tested and rejected the jailbreak reading, and found that user intent in the data (explicit request for insecure code) determines whether misalignment emerges.

doc_summary: A practical guide (co-written with mentees James Chua and John Hughes) on structuring weekly research-meeting slides for empirical LLM work: summary-first framing, agenda, simple bar charts with prompts and error bars, backup slides, and consistent story feedback. It is mostly communication craft and shares field norms, with a few distinctive choices around mentor-facing presentation and scaling-law habits.

contrasts.default: Present results as a polished narrative with conclusions and a full methods walkthrough, showing the complete set of experiments tried.
contrasts.choice: Show only the best or most interesting setup first, put the other setups in backup slides, and include the raw ingredients (prompt, error bars) so the audience can critique the experiment.
contrasts.why: Mentors have little time and energy, and discussing setups that didn't work wastes it; raw ingredients let people critique conclusions that might be wrong.
contrasts.quote: Even though you worked hard to try 10 different experimental setups, you don't show all of them. Show your best setup first, or what your mentor would think is the most interesting.

contrasts.default: Use rich visualizations such as heatmaps to show the full grid of results compactly.
contrasts.choice: Restrict to simple bar charts, with values printed on the bars and at most three model types per slide; treat heatmaps as a negative example.
contrasts.why: Mentors with multiple meetings a day don't have the energy to parse complicated charts.
contrasts.quote: Use simple charts. Mentors who have multiple meetings a day don't have the energy to understand a complicated chart! Stick to easy charts e.g. bar charts.

contrasts.default: Treat a null or failed intervention result as a reason to pivot or report it as negative.
contrasts.choice: Frame the slide so the mentor's role is set by the outcome (debug why it didn't work, e.g. better data or prompts), and prepare data-scaling plots to preempt 'have you tried more data?'.
contrasts.why: The summary frame determines whether the mentor focuses on sanity checks or on debugging.
contrasts.quote: My experiments didn't work. Your mentor will focus on debugging why. E.g., train with better data, or improve the prompts.

contrasts.default: Report results at a single scale without routinely looking for scaling-law behavior.
contrasts.choice: Habitually check for scaling trends, including log-log plots of -log(acc), to enable forecasting.
contrasts.why: Finding predictable scaling trends is helpful for forecasting.
contrasts.quote: Try log-log plots. Not always relevant, so use your judgment, but always keep an eye out for scaling law behavior (if using accuracy, try plotting -log(acc) on the y-axis).

contrasts.default: Treat slide-making as overhead and minimize time spent on it, prioritizing running more experiments.
contrasts.choice: Spend 1-2 days on slides because preparing them surfaces experimental gaps (big error bars, missing controls) that drive the next iteration.
contrasts.why: Doing great experiments is only half the journey; communicating them makes the work matter and improves experimental iteration.
contrasts.quote: The 1-2 days of improving slides helped me to iterate on experimental improvements. E.g. "It seems like my error bars are big here, I need more samples." or "I'm missing a control setup here.

axes.quote: My experiments didn't work. Your mentor will focus on debugging why. E.g., train with better data, or improve the prompts.

new_axes.pole_b: Heavy investment in structured, frequent communication (slides, agenda, story feedback) as part of research

new_axes.name: early-story-framing
new_axes.pole_a: Decide the paper's narrative after results are in
new_axes.pole_b: Iterate on the paper's story in weekly meetings from the start
new_axes.quote: Often getting the paper's story and thinking about how you frame certain elements is left too late. We recommend including slides in your weekly meeting that describe the current story you want to tell so you can get feedback.

doc_summary: A long conceptual and governance paper arguing for AI truthfulness standards (avoiding 'negligent falsehoods'), covering evaluation, institutions, costs/benefits, and technical routes to truthful systems. It runs no experiments and instead lays out an agenda for the field.

contrasts.default: Treat AI honesty/deception as a technical alignment problem about model beliefs and intent, or work on benchmarks and training methods for truthful QA.
contrasts.choice: Frames AI truthfulness as a socio-technical and legal governance problem, proposing standards, certifiers, and adjudicators before the technical capability exists.
contrasts.why: Norms and standards set early may persist 'constitution-like' for decades, so careful early thinking has outsized influence.
contrasts.quote: Work to lay the foundations of how to think about truthfulness, how to build truthful AI, and how to integrate it into our society could increase the likelihood that it is done carefully, and so have outsized influence on what standards are initially adopted.

contrasts.default: Define the target property as honesty (the model asserts only what it believes), the standard framing in alignment work on deception.
contrasts.choice: Deliberately targets truthfulness (outputs match the world) instead of honesty, to avoid dependence on ascribing beliefs to models and to close loopholes such as deluded systems.
contrasts.why: Honesty is hard to evaluate in arbitrary systems and can be satisfied by making the system believe falsehoods.
contrasts.quote: We propose instead a focus on making AI systems only ever make statements that are true, regardless of their beliefs (which we term honesty). We propose instead a focus on making AI systems only ever make statements that are true, regardless of their beliefs (which we term truthfulness).

contrasts.default: Define deception or lying via intent to deceive, as in the human case, or avoid the word for models lacking beliefs.
contrasts.choice: Redefines 'lie' for AI as a falsehood strategically selected and optimised for the speaker's benefit with little optimisation toward truth, with no reference to belief or intent.
contrasts.why: The harms of lying do not hinge on whether an AI system can be said to believe its claims, and many systems cannot be ascribed beliefs.
contrasts.quote: Thus, in the context of AI systems, we define a “lie” as a false statement that has been strongly strategically selected and optimised for the speaker’s benefit, with little or no optimisation pressure going towards making it truthful.

contrasts.default: Evaluate AI systems with fixed benchmarks or accuracy metrics, or propose a single scalable-oversight method.
contrasts.choice: Proposes an institutional evaluation design in which negligence is judged against other contemporaneous AI systems and tiered limited-versus-full adjudication, with standards that ratchet upward over time.
contrasts.why: Society cannot penalise what AI could not feasibly have known, and standards should rise as capability grows.
contrasts.quote: Thus, a society could start out with lenient norms (when AI falsehoods are easily detectable and typically do not cause much harm), and gradually make them more demanding.

contrasts.default: Present a research agenda in a purely technical register, focused on feasible near-term methods.
contrasts.choice: Includes explicit analysis of political capture, censorship, and ossification of belief as first-order risks of truthfulness standards themselves.
contrasts.why: Nobody has full knowledge of the truth, so any arbiter mechanism would make errors and could be captured.
contrasts.quote: A worrying possibility is that enshrining some particular mechanism as an arbiter of truth would forestall our ability to have open-minded, varied, self-correcting approaches to discovering what’s true.

contrasts.default: Stay with concrete near-term technical work and avoid committing to speculation about superhuman systems and decades-out dynamics.
contrasts.choice: Reasons explicitly about regimes where AI exceeds human evaluators, and about the speculative argument that language modelling and RL will not yield truthful systems by default.
contrasts.why: Evaluators must understand topics at least as well as the systems they evaluate; otherwise they must penalise or trust blindly.
contrasts.quote: In summary, we have a speculative argument that language modelling (without tweaks or modifications) is unlikely to produce truthful AI systems.

axes.quote: A more narrow target is to have AI systems avoid stating falsehoods. In particular, this target would disregard why an AI system made their statement, disregard how any particular listener reacts to the statement.
We would like to have the best possible understanding of the tradeoffs when people are making those decisions.
Ultimately, we expect practical experience to be essential for finding effective evaluation methods, and such experience may invalidate some of the ideas presented here.

new_axes.name: conceptual vs empirical framing
new_axes.pole_a: Conceptual, governance and institutional analysis before technical systems exist
new_axes.pole_b: Empirical experiments and benchmarks on current models
new_axes.quote: Analysis from our armchairs is at serious risk of missing important considerations. And implementing a badly designed system could have serious consequences.

new_axes.name: timing of norm-setting
new_axes.pole_a: Shape standards and institutions early, anticipating future capabilities
new_axes.pole_b: Wait until capabilities and harms are concrete before proposing governance
new_axes.quote: This is a time when norms and standards will be established — deliberately or organically. This could be done carefully or in reaction to a hot-button issue of the day.

doc_summary: An Open Philanthropy RFP post proposing research on truthful AI (avoids falsehoods) and honest AI (asserts only what it believes), covering definitions, benchmarks, techniques and interpretability. It frames the area as new and motivated by both alignment and societal benefits, and leaves priorities open.

contrasts.default: Treat truthfulness as factual accuracy or hallucination reduction, a standard NLP benchmark target, without separating it from what the model believes.
contrasts.choice: Splits truthfulness (avoiding falsehoods) from honesty (asserting only what the model believes), allowing a model to be one without the other, and treats honesty as the alignment-relevant property.
contrasts.why: Honest reporting of consequences could be integrated into reward signals when humans cannot evaluate complex behavior.
contrasts.quote: A system can be honest but not truthful. If an honest system believes the Earth is flat, then it can say this without violating honesty. Conversely, a system can be truthful but not honest.

contrasts.default: Study honesty only once models are capable enough to have clear beliefs or goals, or avoid it as too philosophically fuzzy for ML.
contrasts.choice: Proposes studying whether honesty generalizes today, using translator models trained to report beliefs on some categories and tested on held-out ones, plus Go-playing models answering questions.
contrasts.why: Experiments with current models might shed light on whether training honesty on some beliefs transfers to others.
contrasts.quote: a translator model could be trained to translate several different categories of text, then trained to honestly report its beliefs about some of those categories. The model could then be tested on how honestly it reports its beliefs about the other categories.

contrasts.default: Treat calibration as the match between token or completion probabilities and correctness.
contrasts.choice: Argues calibration should apply to claims or beliefs rather than specific string completions, and that models should verbalize confidence that matches correctness.
contrasts.why: What matters is how likely it is to rain, not how likely the string 'Next week it will rain' is.
contrasts.quote: But we may care more about the calibration of claims or beliefs rather than specific completions. For example, how likely is it to rain next week (according to the model’s belief) rather than how likely are strings like “Next week it will rain”.

contrasts.default: Present a focused agenda with prioritized, concrete projects, treating definitions and benchmarks as prerequisites to techniques.
contrasts.choice: Explicitly declines to prioritize definitions or benchmarks, says techniques work needs neither, and asks applicants to refine and generate their own questions.
contrasts.why: The area is new and it is hard to say which projects are most promising.
contrasts.quote: However, we do not assign any priority to (1) or (2). A good project may focus on (3) -- developing techniques for improving truthfulness -- and this would not require novel research on definitions or benchmarks.

contrasts.default: Test truthfulness only on current, human-checkable domains, since future superhuman topics cannot be tested.
contrasts.choice: Suggests simulating the shift from topics humans understand to those they don't, to test robust truthfulness in current models.
contrasts.why: This cannot be tested directly with current models but can probably be usefully simulated.
contrasts.quote: It’s also valuable to understand whether models remain truthful when shifting from topics that we humans understand well to topics we don’t. This cannot be tested directly with current models, but it can probably be usefully simulated

axes.quote: Research on truthful models motivated by alignment/safety is a new area. It is difficult to say which projects are most promising. We will describe a number of research questions that seem promising to us but these should be taken as suggestions that are not set in stone.
Definitions could cover a range of settings (e.g. long-form texts, dialogue) and also address features of statements like ambiguity, uncertainty, figurative language, etc.
Nonetheless, we think it’s plausible that techniques developed now could teach us something about how to make future models honest and truthful.

new_axes.name: Honesty vs accuracy framing
new_axes.pole_a: Evaluate outputs against ground truth (factual accuracy)
new_axes.pole_b: Evaluate whether outputs match the model's internal beliefs, including via interpretability
new_axes.quote: For assessing both the truthfulness and honesty of models, it would be valuable to better understand what a model “believes” and how models represent the world.

new_axes.name: Agenda openness
new_axes.pole_a: Prescribe specific projects and priorities
new_axes.pole_b: Seed broad directions and fund researchers to generate their own questions
new_axes.quote: We are looking to fund people with a willingness to independently refine research questions and to generate their own novel questions.

doc_summary: TruthfulQA is an 817-question benchmark hand-written to elicit 'imitative falsehoods' (false answers that are likely under the training distribution), showing that larger GPT-family models are less truthful. The paper builds the benchmark around a theoretical prediction of inverse scaling and then runs controls and paraphrase tests to separate imitative from non-imitative failures.

contrasts.default: Measure factual accuracy or hallucination on QA, treating all false answers as one error class that scaling should reduce.
contrasts.choice: Isolated a specific mechanistic category, 'imitative falsehoods' (false answers incentivized by the training objective), and built a benchmark to target only that.
contrasts.why: Imitative falsehoods are less likely to be covered by existing QA benchmarks, and scaling laws predict they should get worse with scale, so they are not solved by scaling.
contrasts.quote: Another reason is that scaling laws suggest that scaling up models will reduce perplexity on the training distribution (Kaplan et al., 2020). This will decrease the rate of falsehoods that arise from not learning the distribution well enough

contrasts.default: Collect questions from natural sources or crowdsourcing, or write them without regard to a particular model's behaviour.
contrasts.choice: Hand-wrote questions on the premise that some humans would answer falsely, adversarially filtered against GPT-3-175B, then wrote an additional unfiltered set using what was learned.
contrasts.why: To target a weakness in truthfulness (imitation of human falsehoods) rather than test a useful task.
contrasts.quote: We wrote questions that some humans would answer falsely. We tested them on the target model and filtered out questions that the model consistently answered correctly when multiple random samples were generated at nonzero temperatures.

contrasts.default: Report the inverse scaling result as the headline finding and infer the cause (imitation) from the scaling trend, or treat the adversarial filtering as a possible artifact without testing it.
contrasts.choice: Explicitly stated that adversarial filtering might make the result a non-imitative artifact, then ran several independent tests (transfer to unfiltered GPT-Neo/J, matched one-to-three-word-edit control questions, paraphrases) to discriminate.
contrasts.why: Questions built adversarially against GPT-3 may exploit syntax or style weaknesses rather than imitation of training text.
contrasts.quote: We ran an experiment testing models on matched control questions. Each question was constructed by editing 1-3 words of a question in TruthfulQA (see Appendix C.2 for examples).

contrasts.default: Define truthfulness as correctness and score non-answers as failures, to avoid a trivially gameable metric.
contrasts.choice: Defined truthfulness as avoiding false assertions, so 'No comment' counts as true, and paired it with a separate informativeness score, analogous to precision/recall.
